title: Code Quality Automation
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of code quality automation and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to code quality automation.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on code quality automation. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Code Quality Automation matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. A quality workflow can run project linters, formatters, static analysis, and configuration checks; a failing tool exit code should be visible to reviewers. A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A quality workflow can run project linters, formatters, static analysis, and configuration checks; a failing tool exit code should be visible to reviewers. A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Linters
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

items.title: Formatters
items.text: Use `${{ ... }}` for workflow expressions and the correct context for the field. Treat event-derived values as data: pass untrusted text through an environment variable and quote it instead of inserting it into shell source.

items.title: Static analysis
items.text: For static analysis, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Configuration validation
items.text: For configuration validation, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Enforcing project conventions
items.text: For enforcing project conventions, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Publishing quality reports
items.text: Trace the release to a source commit, validate the selected version/ref, restrict publication permissions, retain build evidence, and verify the published artifact before promoting it.

content_blocks.code:
name: Lint and static checks
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
content_blocks.expected_output: The job installs locked dependencies and runs the project lint command; a non-zero lint status fails the job.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a JavaScript project that defines `lint` in `package.json` and has a committed lockfile.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Adapt the package manager and lint command to the actual project; do not hide a failing lint exit code.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to code quality automation. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain code quality automation, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Build CI checks that produce repeatable evidence and protect merge quality.

content.task: Apply code quality automation to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: A quality workflow can run project linters, formatters, static analysis, and configuration checks; a failing tool exit code should be visible to reviewers.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: A quality workflow can run project linters, formatters, static analysis, and configuration checks; a failing tool exit code should be visible to reviewers. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: A quality workflow can run project linters, formatters, static analysis, and configuration checks; a failing tool exit code should be visible to reviewers.

A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
